title: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
summary: How pretraining loss follows power laws in size, data and FLOPs, how to split a budget, fit your own scaling law with error bars, set batch size and data repeats, and when to train past compute-optimal.
outcomes: Explain why a power law is a straight line on log-log axes and what its exponent means
Compute training compute with C = 6ND and trade parameters against tokens at a fixed budget
Find the compute-optimal model size from an IsoFLOP curve or the Chinchilla closed form
Design a scaling sweep, fit it two ways, and bootstrap error bars on the extrapolation
Explain why Kaplan and Chinchilla disagreed and why GPT-3-era models were undertrained
Pick batch size and learning rate as compute grows, and plan training when unique data runs short
Decide when to train past compute-optimal because of inference cost, and spot where scaling laws mislead

lessons.title: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space

blocks.md: You know from the pretraining course that a language model is trained to minimize next-token cross-entropy loss, measured in nats per token. A **nat** is the unit you get when that loss uses the natural log: the loss at one position is $-\ln p$, where $p$ is the probability the model gave the true next token, so a loss of 1 nat means $p = 1/e$, about 0.37, and 1 nat is about 1.44 bits. A frontier pretraining run costs months of accelerator time (thousands of GPUs or TPUs), and you usually get one attempt. Before spending that budget you must decide how many parameters the model gets and how many tokens it reads, and you would like to know roughly what loss it will reach.

Trial and error at full scale is unaffordable, and intuition fails because loss improves slowly and unevenly. A **scaling law** is the alternative: an empirical formula, fitted to many cheap small runs, that predicts how loss changes as you scale **model size** $N$ (parameters), **data** $D$ (training tokens) and **compute** $C$ (training FLOPs). If the formula holds over several orders of magnitude, you can extrapolate it to the run you cannot afford to repeat.

Kaplan et al. (2020) trained Transformers from 768 to 1.5 billion non-embedding parameters on WebText2 and found that, when the other two factors are not the bottleneck, loss follows a **power law** in each of $N$, $D$ and $C$. **Non-embedding** parameters are all the weights except the token-embedding table (one learned vector per vocabulary entry) and the position embeddings. For a Transformer with $n_{layer}$ layers of width $d_{model}$ that is about $12\,n_{layer} d_{model}^2$: per layer, $4d_{model}^2$ for the four attention projections plus $8d_{model}^2$ for the two feed-forward matrices of size $d_{model} \times 4d_{model}$. The paper found that leaving out the embeddings gives much cleaner trends. **WebText2** is OpenAI's web-text corpus: pages linked from Reddit posts that got at least 3 karma (net upvotes), about 23 billion tokens. The trends held across eight orders of magnitude in compute and six in model size. For model size the fit is:

blocks.caption: Kaplan et al. Eq. 1.1. In words: loss equals N_c divided by N, raised to the power alpha_N. N_c, about 8.8e13, is the size at which the formula would predict a loss of 1 nat. N counts non-embedding parameters; models trained on enough data to not overfit.

blocks.md: Take logs of both sides: $\log L = \alpha_N \log N_c - \alpha_N \log N$. That is a straight line in $\log N$ with slope $-\alpha_N$. So on log-log axes a power law looks like a ruler-straight line, which is exactly what the paper's plots show. Both constants are fitted, not derived: Kaplan et al. chose $\alpha_N \approx 0.076$ and $N_c$ so the line passes through their measured runs, and $N_c$ has no physical meaning because it shifts with the tokenizer. The exponent $\alpha_N$ is the whole story: it says how fast loss falls per multiplicative step in size. Making the model 10 times larger multiplies $L$ by $10^{-\alpha_N} = 10^{-0.076}$, about 0.839.

blocks.title: Kaplan's L(N) with a movable model size

scenes.caption: At N = 10 million parameters the fit predicts a loss of 3.371 nats per token.
Ten times more parameters (100 million): loss 2.83. The loss was multiplied by 0.839.
1 billion: loss 2.376. Again multiplied by 0.839. Every 10x step gives the same ratio, which is why the curve is gently bent here but straight on log-log axes.
10 billion: loss 1.994. Drag the slider: the predicted gain per 10x never changes in ratio, but the absolute drop shrinks.

blocks.prompt: With $\alpha_N = 0.076$, doubling $N$ multiplies loss by $2^{-0.076}$. How many times larger must the model be to **halve** the loss, if this law kept holding?
blocks.reveal: About **9,100 times** larger, because $2^{1/0.076} \approx 9,139$. Doubling alone multiplies loss by only 0.949, about a 5% cut (the paper quotes 0.95). Small exponents mean huge multiplicative scale-ups for modest loss gains, which is why scaling is a compute story.

blocks.title: Same ratio per 10x, shrinking absolute gains

scenes.caption: Predicted loss at each size from the Kaplan fit. Each bar is the previous one times 0.839.
The absolute drops per 10x shrink: 0.541, 0.454, 0.381, 0.32. Constant ratio, diminishing absolute returns.

blocks.md: The same paper fits two more single-factor laws. For **data**, it trains models large enough that size is not the bottleneck on $D$ tokens with **early stopping**: training halts when the loss on held-out text stops falling, before the model starts to memorize its small dataset. For **compute**, it uses $C_{min}$, the compute of a run whose model size is chosen optimally for its budget and whose batch is well below the critical batch size (lesson 6), so no FLOPs are wasted.

blocks.caption: Kaplan et al. Eqs. 1.2 and 1.3. Same shape as L(N), different exponents. A PF-day is 8.64e19 FLOPs (lesson 2 explains it); with this law 1 PF-day predicts 2.66 nats, 100 PF-days 2.11 and 10,000 PF-days 1.68.

blocks.md: Real runs are limited by $N$ and $D$ at once, so Kaplan et al. also fit a joint law, $L(N, D) = \left[(N_c/N)^{\alpha_N/\alpha_D} + D_c/D\right]^{\alpha_D}$, refitted for this form as $\alpha_N = 0.076$, $\alpha_D = 0.103$, $N_c = 6.4 \times 10^{13}$, $D_c = 1.8 \times 10^{13}$. With unlimited data it reduces to $L(N)$, with an unlimited model to $L(D)$. In between it says when a model of a given size starts to **overfit**, doing better on its training text than on new text, because it has too few tokens. Their rule: to keep the loss within about 2 percent of $L(N)$, roughly the run-to-run variation they saw between random seeds, use $D \gtrsim 5 \times 10^{3}\, N^{0.74}$ tokens. For 1B parameters that is 23B tokens, which is why their models under 1B showed little overfitting on the 22B training tokens of WebText2.

blocks.title: Kaplan's joint law: data limits a model of fixed size

scenes.caption: All three curves use the joint fit's constants. Without a model-size limit, loss falls as a power law in D: a straight line on log-log axes.
A 100M model cannot follow that line forever. Its joint-law curve bends onto its own floor L(N) = 2.762: 2.957 at 1B tokens, 2.788 at 10B.
At the dashed line (4.2B tokens for 100M parameters) the loss is 2.821, about 2 percent above the floor. Past it, more data still helps, but very little.
A 1B model: floor 2.319, and the dashed line moves out to 23B tokens (loss 2.368). At 10B tokens it sits at 2.420. Bigger models need more data, but only as N^0.74.

blocks.md: A pure power law heads to zero loss, which is impossible: text has irreducible randomness, so loss cannot fall below the entropy of the data. Kaplan et al. note the trend **must flatten out eventually**. Later fits (lesson 3) add a constant floor $E$. Also, loss values depend on the dataset and tokenizer, so numbers from different papers are not comparable.

A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

blocks.question: A run at 100M non-embedding parameters reaches the loss Kaplan's fit predicts (2.83). Using the same law with ample data, what loss should a 10B model reach?
options: About 2.38
About 1.42, half the loss for 100x the size
About 1.99
About 2.83 minus 2 x 0.45, so 1.92
blocks.explain: Two 10x steps, each multiplying loss by 0.839: $2.83 \times 0.839^2 \approx 1.99$. 2.38 is only one step (1B). Subtracting a fixed amount per step assumes a linear trend, and halving would need about 9,139x more parameters, not 100x.

blocks.question: On log-log axes, a team's loss-versus-parameters points lie on a straight line with slope -0.07. Which statement is correct?
options: Each doubling of N removes the same fraction of the loss
Each doubling of N removes the same absolute amount of loss
Loss will reach zero at a finite model size
The slope says how much data the model needs
blocks.explain: A straight line in log-log space is a power law: equal multiplicative steps in N give equal multiplicative changes in L, here $2^{-0.07} \approx 0.95$ per doubling. Absolute drops shrink, the curve never reaches zero, and the slope says nothing about data needs on its own.

lessons.title: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND

blocks.md: A scaling law needs a common currency. The budget you actually have is **compute**: a number of floating point operations (FLOPs) you can afford. To compare a big model trained briefly with a small model trained long, you need to convert parameters and tokens into FLOPs.

Start with one token and a model with $N$ parameters. In the forward pass almost every parameter takes part in one multiply and one add for that token, so the forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs. The backward pass does two matrix multiplies for each weight matrix, each as big as the forward one: one gives the gradient for the layer's input, to pass further back, and one gives the gradient for the weights themselves. That is twice the forward cost, $4N$. Total: about $6N$ FLOPs per training token.

blocks.title: Where the 6 in 6ND comes from

scenes.caption: One token flows through the network. Each parameter does roughly one multiply-add: about 2N FLOPs.
Backpropagation computes gradients with respect to activations and weights, roughly twice the forward cost: about 4N FLOPs.
Forward plus backward is about 6N FLOPs per token. Multiplying by D training tokens gives the run's compute.

blocks.caption: In words: training compute is about 6 times parameters times tokens. Kaplan et al. Sec. 2.1. It ignores the attention cost that grows with context length, which is small when d_model is large relative to context length / 12 (derived next).

blocks.md: Where does that 12 come from? Besides the weight multiplies, each token's attention runs over the $n_{ctx}$ positions of its context, which Kaplan et al. count as about $2\,n_{layer} n_{ctx} d_{model}$ FLOPs per forward pass (the score product only; PaLM also counts the weighted sum over values, which doubles it), where $d_{model}$ is the width of each token's vector and $n_{ctx}$ the context length. The weight work is $2N \approx 24\,n_{layer} d_{model}^2$. Dividing the two gives $n_{ctx}/(12\,d_{model})$, so attention is a small extra once $d_{model}$ is well above $n_{ctx}/12$: for GPT-3, width 12,288 and context 2,048, it is about 1.4 percent.

This approximation is what makes the three knobs trade off cleanly. For a fixed budget $C$, choosing $N$ fixes $D = C/(6N)$: a model twice as large can read only half as many tokens. Compute is often quoted in PF-days (petaFLOP/s-days): a machine sustaining $10^{15}$ FLOPs per second (peta means $10^{15}$) for one day of 86,400 seconds, so one PF-day is $10^{15} \times 86400 = 8.64 \times 10^{19}$ FLOPs. Our running example is **Chinchilla**, a 70B-parameter model DeepMind trained in 2022 to test the scaling study you meet in lesson 3, and its comparison point is **Gopher**, DeepMind's 280B model from 2021.

blocks.title: From parameters and tokens to FLOPs and days
blocks.code:
N = 70e9            # parameters (Chinchilla)
D = 1.4e12          # training tokens
per_token = 6 * N   # 2N forward + 4N backward
C = per_token * D   # total training FLOPs
pf_days = C / 8.64e19          # 1 PF-day = 1e15 * 86400
gpus, flops_each = 1000, 4e14  # assumed sustained FLOP/s
days = C / (gpus * flops_each) / 86400
print(f'{C:.3g} FLOPs, {pf_days:.0f} PF-days, {days:.1f} days')

scenes.caption: Chinchilla's configuration: 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens.
6N FLOPs per token.
Times D tokens gives the total training compute.
Converted to PF-days for comparison with the Kaplan paper's units.
Wall-clock depends on hardware and utilization. Simplified: we assume 1000 accelerators each sustaining 4e14 FLOP/s, an illustrative figure, not a measured one.

blocks.md: Apply the same arithmetic to real models. Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens) comes to 5.04e+23 FLOPs by 6ND; the Chinchilla paper reports 5.76e+23 using a more detailed count that includes attention and embeddings. Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) comes to 5.88e+23: the **same budget**, spent on a model 4 times smaller trained on about 4.7 times more tokens. Meta's Llama 3 405B (2024, the third generation of its open LLaMA models) on 15.6T tokens gives 3.79e+25, matching the 3.8e25 Meta reports.

blocks.title: Parameters, tokens and compute of four models

scenes.caption: Parameters in billions. Gopher is four times the size of Chinchilla.
Training tokens in billions. Chinchilla reads 1400B tokens, almost five times Gopher's 300B. LLaMA's smallest model reads 1000B.
Compute by 6ND in units of 1e21 FLOPs: 315, 504, 588, 40. Gopher and Chinchilla cost about the same; they just split it differently.

blocks.prompt: You double both the parameter count and the number of training tokens. By what factor does training compute grow?
blocks.reveal: **4x.** $C \approx 6ND$ is a product, so doubling both multiplies it by $2 \times 2$. This is why scaling both knobs together gets expensive fast, and why the question of how to split a budget between them matters so much.

blocks.md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 7.
$C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

blocks.question: Your budget is fixed. You decide to make the model 3 times larger than planned. What must happen to the number of training tokens?
options: It stays the same, compute depends only on N
It must triple
It must drop to one third
It must drop to one ninth
blocks.explain: With $C \approx 6ND$ fixed, $D = C/(6N)$, so tripling N cuts D to one third. Compute depends on both knobs; nothing about the product is squared.

blocks.question: Using $C \approx 6ND$, roughly how much compute does a 405B-parameter model trained on 15.6T tokens use?
options: About 3.8e25 FLOPs
About 6.3e24 FLOPs
About 1.3e25 FLOPs
About 2.5e26 FLOPs
blocks.explain: $6 \times 4.05\times10^{11} \times 1.56\times10^{13} \approx 3.8e+25$ FLOPs, which matches the 3.8e25 Meta reports for Llama 3 405B. 6.3e24 forgets the factor 6; 1.3e25 uses 2N (inference cost) instead of 6N.

lessons.title: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves

blocks.md: Now the central question. You have a budget $C$. Every choice of $N$ fixes $D = C/(6N)$. Make the model too large and it sees too few tokens to learn what it can represent. Make it too small and it saturates: more tokens stop helping because it lacks capacity. Somewhere in between, loss is lowest. That model is **compute-optimal** for $C$.

Hoffmann et al. (2022), the Chinchilla paper from DeepMind, measured this directly, in three independent ways. **Approach 1** fixes several model sizes, trains each for different numbers of tokens, and at every FLOP count keeps the lowest loss any run reached. **Approach 2** is the **IsoFLOP** approach (iso is Greek for equal, so each curve holds FLOPs equal): they fixed 9 budgets from $6 \times 10^{18}$ to $3 \times 10^{21}$ FLOPs, trained models of many sizes at each budget (with the learning-rate schedule, the planned rise and decay of the step size over training, matched to each run's token count), and recorded the final loss. At each budget, loss against model size is a valley; they located its bottom by fitting a parabola in $\log N$ through that budget's runs (lesson 4 does this in code). **Approach 3**, the parametric fit, fits a single formula to all their runs:

blocks.caption: E: loss of an ideal model (entropy of the text). A/N^alpha: penalty for a finite model. B/D^beta: penalty for finite data and finite optimization.

blocks.md: Hoffmann et al. report $E = 1.69$, $A = 406.4$, $B = 410.7$, $\alpha = 0.34$, $\beta = 0.28$. In this lesson we plot the **refit by Besiroglu et al. (2024)**: $E = 1.8172$, $A = 482.01$, $B = 2085.43$, $\alpha = 0.3478$, $\beta = 0.3658$, fitted to data reconstructed from the Chinchilla paper. We use it because its optimum agrees with Chinchilla's other two methods; lesson 4 shows how such fits are made and why the published one went wrong, and lesson 7 shows how much the two fits' advice differs. This $\alpha$ is not Kaplan's $\alpha_N$ of 0.076: Kaplan fitted the total loss with no floor, while here the constant $E$ is taken out first and only the excess above it follows a power law, which falls much faster. Simplified: losses are for MassiveText, DeepMind's training set of web pages, books, news, code and Wikipedia; only the shape transfers.

blocks.title: Predicted loss over a grid of N and D (refit)

scenes.caption: Each cell is the refit loss for one (N, D) pair. Loss falls toward the bottom right, where both model and data are large.
The anti-diagonal cells all cost the same, 6ND = 6e22 FLOPs. Along it the loss goes 2.21, 2.11, 2.06, 2.05, 2.09, 2.17: a valley, lowest in the middle.
A 10x larger budget, 6e23 FLOPs: 2.01, 1.98, 1.97, 2.0. The valley moves down and to the right: both N and D grow.

blocks.title: IsoFLOP curve: loss vs model size at fixed compute

scenes.caption: C = 1e20 FLOPs. The valley bottoms out at N = 0.85B with D = 19.5B tokens, loss 2.553.
C = 1e21: optimum N = 2.78B, D = 60B, loss 2.306.
C = 1e22: N = 9.05B, D = 184B. Each 10x in compute moves the optimum N by about 3.3x.
Gopher's budget, 5.76e23: the refit's optimum is 72B parameters on 1.33T tokens, close to Chinchilla's 70B on 1.4T.

blocks.prompt: At Gopher's budget the optimum is about 72B parameters with loss 1.974. Which hurts more: a model 4x too **large** (and so 4x fewer tokens), or 4x too **small**?
blocks.reveal: About equally, and only a little: 4x larger and 4x smaller both give about **1.994**, only 0.02 above the minimum. The valley is broad and nearly symmetric in log N. The Llama 3 team observed the same thing: IsoFLOP curves get flatter around the minimum as compute grows, so being somewhat off the optimal size costs little.

blocks.md: Because the formula is a sum of power laws, minimizing it under $C = 6ND$ has a closed form (Hoffmann et al., Eq. 4). Here is the derivation. Substitute $D = C/(6N)$, so loss depends on $N$ alone. Each time you multiply $N$ by a small factor, the model penalty $A/N^{\alpha}$ falls at rate $\alpha A/N^{\alpha}$, and because $D$ shrinks by the same factor the data penalty $B/D^{\beta}$ rises at rate $\beta B/D^{\beta}$. Loss is lowest where the two rates balance, $\alpha A/N^{\alpha} = \beta B/D^{\beta}$. Solving that for $N$ gives:

blocks.tex: N_{opt}(C) = G\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{a},\quad D_{opt}(C) = G^{-1}\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{b},\quad G = \left(\frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}},\ a = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},\ b = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
blocks.caption: In words: the optimal size is a constant G times C over 6 to the power a, with a equal to beta over (alpha plus beta). Tokens follow from D = C/(6N), which leaves exponent b, alpha over (alpha plus beta), so a plus b is 1.

blocks.md: With the refit, $G \approx 0.120$, $a = 0.513$ and $b = 0.487$. At 1e22 FLOPs the balance holds: 0.348 times the model penalty 0.166 and 0.366 times the data penalty 0.158 both come to 0.058. Parameters and tokens grow at almost the same rate, each roughly as $\sqrt{C}$. The resulting ratio is about 20 tokens per parameter (20.4 at 1e22 FLOPs, 18.4 at 5.76e23). Chinchilla's own table (Approach 1) says the same: 1B parameters wants 20.2B tokens, 10B wants 205.1B, 67B wants 1.5T.
Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

Compute-optimal means lowest loss **per training FLOP**. It says nothing about the cost of serving the model afterwards, and the 20x ratio is tied to the data, architecture and training recipe it was measured on.

blocks.question: Under Chinchilla-style scaling (N and D each proportional to about $C^{0.5}$), your compute budget grows 10x. How should the model size change?
options: Grow about 10x, keeping tokens fixed
Grow about 5.4x
Grow about 3.2x, and tokens about 3.2x too
Stay fixed and train 10x longer
blocks.explain: $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$ for both N and D, and $3.16 \times 3.16 = 10$ recovers the 10x compute. 5.4x is the Kaplan prescription ($10^{0.73}$) from lesson 5. Putting all of it into one knob walks up a wall of the IsoFLOP valley.

blocks.question: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does loss rise again for the largest models at a fixed budget?
options: Large models overfit any dataset
With compute fixed, a larger N leaves fewer tokens, so the data term B/D^beta grows
Large models have a larger irreducible loss E
Backward passes cost more than forward passes
blocks.explain: At fixed C, $D = C/(6N)$. Pushing N up shrinks D, and the finite-data penalty grows faster than the finite-model penalty falls. E is the same for every model, and the 6N cost is already accounted for in the budget.

lessons.title: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars

blocks.md:
Lesson 3 read compute-optimal sizes off smooth curves. A real study gives you something rougher: a handful of finished runs, each with one noisy final loss. Here is one budget, $10^{19}$ FLOPs, with 7 model sizes a factor of 2 apart, from 33M to 2.1B parameters. Their final losses are 3.218, 3.050, 2.950, 2.921, 2.970, 3.088 and 3.248. The lowest *run* is the 262M model, but the true optimum could sit anywhere near it. This lesson turns runs like these into a law you can extrapolate, and puts error bars on it.

The runs in this lesson are synthetic: we generate them from lesson 3's refit plus Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 0.02 nats (seeded), so we know the true answer and can check every fit. Everything was computed on a laptop CPU.

**Designing the sweep.** Published studies share a recipe:

- **Budgets** spanning at least two orders of magnitude. Chinchilla used 9 from $6 \times 10^{18}$ to $3 \times 10^{21}$ FLOPs; Llama 3 used $6 \times 10^{18}$ to $10^{22}$ with models from 40M to 16B; DeepSeek LLM used 8 budgets from $10^{17}$ to $3 \times 10^{20}$ with about 10 splits each.
- **Sizes** at each budget spread wide enough to show a clear minimum, with runs on both walls of the valley.
- **A schedule per run.** Each run's learning-rate decay should end at its own last token (Chinchilla matched the cosine length to the target FLOPs); lesson 5 shows what a shared schedule did to Kaplan's fit. A cheaper option from Hägele et al. (2024) is one constant-rate run per size with short cooldowns branched off; the optional *WSD learning-rate schedules* course covers it, but this lesson does not need it.

Our study: 5 budgets from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$, 7 sizes per budget from 1/8 to 8 times the true optimum, 35 runs.

blocks.title: One IsoFLOP budget (1e19 FLOPs): noisy runs and a parabola

scenes.caption: Seven finished runs at 1e19 FLOPs. Noise makes the valley ragged: the lowest run (262M) is only the best of the sizes you happened to try.
Fit a parabola in log10 N through all seven. Its vertex is at 245M parameters with predicted loss 2.926. Every run contributes, so one noisy point moves the answer less.

The true valley bottoms out at 262M (loss 2.927). The lowest run hits it only because we centred the sizes on the truth; a real sweep cannot. The vertex can fall between sizes, but it is a local approximation, worse far up the walls.

blocks.md: **Approach 2, step by step.** With $x = \log_{10} N$, fit $L \approx p_0 x^2 + p_1 x + p_2$ to each budget's runs by least squares. The vertex is that budget's estimated optimum; $p_0$ must come out positive, or the runs show no valley at all. Then fit a straight line through the five points ($\log_{10} C$, vertex). Its slope is the exponent $a$ in $N_{opt} \propto C^a$, and you extend the line to the budget you care about.

blocks.caption: In words: the parabola's lowest point is at minus p1 over 2 p0; a straight line through those points in log-log space is the scaling law for the optimal size.

blocks.title: From five vertices to a forecast four decades away

scenes.caption: The five vertices, one per budget, from 79M at 1e18 to 816M at 1e20. They wobble around a line because each came from noisy runs.
A least-squares line through them has slope 0.512. Extended four orders of magnitude past the largest run, it forecasts 93.4B parameters at 1e24 FLOPs.
The truth for this synthetic study is 95.9B (slope 0.513), so the fit is 2.5 percent low. With real runs you never see the truth line, so you need error bars instead.

blocks.md: **Approach 3, step by step.** Fit all 35 runs at once to $L = E + A/N^{\alpha} + B/D^{\beta}$, the way Hoffmann et al. did. Three details matter. They fit the **log** of the loss, so a 1 percent miss counts the same at every scale. They write $A = e^{a}$, $B = e^{b}$, $E = e^{e}$ (this $a$ is just $\log A$, not the exponent $a$ of $N_{opt} \propto C^a$ from earlier in this lesson), so the log of the prediction is a **log-sum-exp** (LSE, $\log(e^{u} + e^{v} + e^{w})$) of three terms, which keeps all three positive. And they minimize the **Huber loss** of the residuals with $\delta = 10^{-3}$: squared for small errors, linear for large ones, so a few outlier runs cannot drag the fit. The optimizer is **L-BFGS** (limited-memory BFGS, named for Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb and Shanno, who published its update rule; scipy's `L-BFGS-B` variant also allows bounds), a quasi-Newton method that estimates curvature from recent gradients, started from a grid of initial guesses because the objective has several local minima.

blocks.tex: \min_{a,b,e,\alpha,\beta} \sum_i \mathrm{Huber}_{\delta}\Big(\mathrm{LSE}\big(a - \alpha \log N_i,\ b - \beta \log D_i,\ e\big) - \log L_i\Big),\quad \mathrm{Huber}_{\delta}(r) = \begin{cases} r^2/2 & |r| \le \delta \\ \delta\,(|r| - \delta/2) & |r| > \delta \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Hoffmann et al., Appendix D.2, with delta = 1e-3. Each residual is the gap between predicted and observed log loss for run i.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np, itertools
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import logsumexp, huber
E,A,B,al,be = 1.8172,482.01,2085.43,0.3478,0.3658  # truth
L = lambda N,D: E + A/N**al + B/D**be
Nopt = lambda C: 0.11963*(C/6)**0.51261
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); runs = []
for C in [1e18,3e18,1e19,3e19,1e20]:      # 5 budgets
    for k in range(-3,4):                 # 7 sizes per budget
        N = Nopt(C)*2.0**k; D = C/(6*N)
        runs.append((C,N,D,L(N,D)+rng.normal(0,0.02)))
r = np.array(runs); x = np.log10(r[:,1])
# Approach 2: parabola per IsoFLOP curve, then a line
mins = []
for C in np.unique(r[:,0]):
    m = r[:,0]==C; p = np.polyfit(x[m], r[m,3], 2)
    mins.append(-p[1]/(2*p[0]))
a2,b2 = np.polyfit(np.log10(np.unique(r[:,0])), mins, 1)
print(f"A2: a={a2:.3f}  N_opt(1e24)={10**(24*a2+b2):.3g}")
# Approach 3: Huber on log loss, L-BFGS, grid of starts
def obj(p):
    a,b,e,alpha,beta = p
    pred = logsumexp([a-alpha*np.log(r[:,1]),
        b-beta*np.log(r[:,2]), e+0*r[:,1]], axis=0)
    return huber(1e-3, pred-np.log(r[:,3])).sum()
grid = itertools.product([0,10,20],[0,10,20],[-1,0,1],[.5,1.5],[.5,1.5])
tol = dict(ftol=1e-15, gtol=1e-12, maxiter=20000)
fit = min((minimize(obj,g,method="L-BFGS-B",options=tol)
           for g in grid), key=lambda f: f.fun)
a,b,e,alpha,beta = fit.x
G = (alpha*np.exp(a)/(beta*np.exp(b)))**(1/(alpha+beta))
ea = beta/(alpha+beta)
print(f"A3: E={np.exp(e):.3f} alpha={alpha:.3f} beta={beta:.3f}"
      f" a={ea:.3f}  N_opt(1e24)={G*(1e24/6)**ea:.3g}")
blocks.caption: Real output (laptop CPU, about 6 s): A2: a=0.512 N_opt(1e24)=9.34e+10, then A3: E=1.836 alpha=0.358 beta=0.370 a=0.508 N_opt(1e24)=8.91e+10. Truth: a=0.513, 9.59e+10. Hoffmann et al. used 4,500 starting points; 108 suffice here.

blocks.prompt: Both fits land within about 7 percent of the truth (95.9B). Suppose you threw away all 35 runs and repeated the whole study with fresh noise, 200 times. How widely would the Approach 2 forecast at $10^{24}$ FLOPs spread?
blocks.reveal: The middle 80 percent ran from **77B to 115B** for Approach 2, and 77B to 113B for Approach 3: roughly plus or minus 20 percent, from 0.02 nats of noise per run alone. You cannot repeat a real study 200 times. The bootstrap, next, estimates this spread from the one study you have.

blocks.md:
**Error bars with the bootstrap.** Draw 35 runs from your 35 *with replacement* (some appear twice, some not at all), refit, record the forecast, and repeat a few hundred times. The spread of those forecasts estimates how much the answer depends on which runs you happened to get. On our one study, 300 bootstrap refits gave an 80 percent range of 70B to 104B for Approach 2 and 77B to 109B for Approach 3, close to the true repeat-the-study spread.

Besiroglu et al. ran 4,000 bootstraps on 240 points reconstructed from the Chinchilla paper and got a standard error of 0.018 on the exponent $a$. Hoffmann et al. had reported an interval of 0.454 to 0.455; Besiroglu et al. estimate that one so narrow would need about 600,000 runs.

blocks.title: How sweep design changes the forecast (200 repeated studies)

scenes.caption: Width of the 80 percent range of Approach 2's forecast at 1e24 FLOPs, in billions of parameters. The baseline (5 budgets over 100x, 7 sizes from 1/8x to 8x) spans 77B to 115B.
Only 3 sizes within 2x of the optimum barely curve, so the parabola's p0 is poorly pinned and its vertex swings: forecasts from 21B to 358B.
Budgets over only 10x: the same line is extended further relative to its base, so the range widens to 69B to 128B.
Now the median forecasts (truth 95.9B). Sizes all below the optimum bias Approach 2 low, to 75B: its parabola is fitted to one wall, where the valley is not parabolic.
Back to range widths, now for Approach 3. It fits the whole formula, so on the one-sided sweep it is unbiased (median 96.5B, width 47B). The narrow sweep is still its worst case (width 181B).

blocks.md:
**A fit that silently stops early.** Run the same Approach 3 objective with scipy's default L-BFGS-B tolerances from a single start. From one start it returned $a = 0.452$ (a forecast of 47B), from another $a = 0.532$ (124B), and both reported convergence. With tight tolerances (`ftol=1e-15`, `gtol=1e-12`) all five starts we tried reached the same $a = 0.508$. The cause: the summed Huber values are tiny (about $1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ at the optimum), so the default stopping tests on relative improvement and gradient size fire before the parameters settle.

Besiroglu et al. traced the published Chinchilla Approach 3 fit to the same kind of failure. A Chinchilla author confirmed they had averaged the Huber terms instead of summing them, and the optimizer stopped before converging, both in the main fit and in the bootstraps that produced the narrow interval.

Never report a scaling-law forecast without two checks: refit from several starts with tight tolerances and confirm they agree, and bootstrap the runs to get a range. A single unconverged fit can be off by 2x and still look perfectly reasonable.

A scaling study is an experiment design problem: budgets spread over orders of magnitude, sizes that bracket each valley, a properly ended schedule per run, then two fits (IsoFLOP parabolas and the parametric form) that should agree, each with bootstrap error bars.

blocks.question: At one budget your sweep trained only models smaller than the optimum, so the losses fall steadily and never turn up. What happens if you fit a parabola in $\log N$ to them?
options: The vertex lands on the optimum, because a parabola extrapolates the valley exactly
The fit raises an error, so you will notice the problem
Nothing; Approach 2 does not depend on which sizes you train
The vertex is extrapolated off one wall of a valley that is not exactly parabolic, so it can be biased
blocks.explain: In our repeated studies, sizes from 1/64x to 1x of the optimum pulled Approach 2's median forecast down to 75B against a truth of 96B, with no error raised. Approach 3, which fits the full formula to all runs, was not biased. Bracket each valley on both sides.

blocks.question: Why did Hoffmann et al. minimize a Huber loss on log loss rather than plain squared error on the loss itself?
options: The log makes a 1 percent miss count equally at every scale, and Huber keeps a few outlier runs from dominating
Huber loss makes L-BFGS converge in a single step
Squared error cannot be minimized with gradients
Taking logs removes the need to fit the constant E
blocks.explain: Losses differ across scales, so log residuals put every run on equal footing. Huber is quadratic within delta and linear beyond it, so one bad run pulls with bounded force; Hoffmann et al. found that important for predicting held-out larger runs. E is still fitted, as one of the three LSE terms.

blocks.question: Your Approach 3 fit gives $a = 0.45$ from one starting point and $a = 0.53$ from another, and both report success. What is the most likely problem?
options: The functional form is wrong, so no fit can be trusted
You need more model sizes per budget before fitting
The optimizer stopped before converging: tighten tolerances, sum rather than average the loss, and compare several starts
Noise is too high; average the two answers
blocks.explain: Two different answers on the same data mean at least one run never reached a minimum. In our example both starts settled on a = 0.508 once tolerances were tight. Averaging two unconverged fits fixes nothing, and the form itself fits these runs well.

lessons.title: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained

blocks.md: Kaplan et al. (2020) asked the same question and reached a different answer. Their fit said the optimal model size grows as $N \propto C^{0.73}$ while data grows only as $D \propto C^{0.27}$ (the two exponents add to 1 because $C \approx 6ND$). Their summary: for a fixed budget you get the best loss by **training very large models and stopping significantly short of convergence**, that is, before the loss has flattened out.

That advice shaped the large models that followed. Chinchilla's Table 1 lists OpenAI's GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens), Gopher (280B, 300B) and MT-NLG (Megatron-Turing NLG from Microsoft and NVIDIA, 530B, 270B): most large models of the time were trained on roughly 300B tokens regardless of size. Hoffmann et al. (2022) found instead that $N$ and $D$ should grow at about the same rate: exponents 0.50 and 0.50 (Approach 1), 0.49 and 0.51 (IsoFLOP), 0.46 and 0.54 (parametric fit).

blocks.title: How each law spends extra compute

scenes.caption: Kaplan's prescription: most extra compute goes into parameters. At 1000x compute, the model grows about 155x (1000^0.73).
Under Kaplan, tokens grow only about 6.5x (1000^0.27) for that same 1000x, so tokens per parameter keep falling as models grow.
Chinchilla: both grow about 31.6x (1000^0.5, the square root) per 1000x compute, so the tokens-per-parameter ratio stays roughly constant.

blocks.prompt: Gopher used 5.76e23 FLOPs on 280B parameters and 300B tokens. Chinchilla's analysis said the optimal model for that budget is about 4x smaller on about 4x more tokens. What happened when they trained it?
blocks.reveal: Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens, same budget) **beat Gopher** across the board. On MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding: four-option multiple-choice questions in 57 subjects, asked 5-shot, meaning five solved examples are placed in the prompt first) it scored 67.6% against Gopher's 60.0%. It is also 4x cheaper to run per token, since inference cost scales with N.

blocks.title: Training tokens per parameter

scenes.caption: The Kaplan-era models: 0.51, 1.07 and 1.71 tokens per parameter.
Chinchilla: 1.4T tokens on 70B parameters, 20 tokens per parameter, the compute-optimal ratio.
Later models go further: Llama 3 405B at 38.5, and LLaMA's smallest model at about 149 (1T tokens on 6.7B). Lesson 7 explains why going past 20 can be deliberate.

blocks.md:
Why did Kaplan's fit point the wrong way? Three explanations, each from a paper that re-ran the analysis:

1. **Learning-rate schedule.** Kaplan used one schedule length for all runs and read losses off intermediate checkpoints. A cosine schedule lowers the learning rate along half a cosine wave, from its peak to a small final value at the planned last step. Hoffmann et al. showed it should be matched to the run's token count; mid-run checkpoints of a longer schedule show a higher loss than a properly scheduled short run reaches, which makes training on more tokens look less useful than it is.
2. **What counts as a parameter, and scale.** Pearce and Song (2024) found that counting only non-embedding parameters, combined with mostly small models, biases the fitted exponent toward Kaplan's value.

**3. Training details.** Porian et al. (2024) reproduced Kaplan's law, then removed it by accounting for last-layer compute (the final layer that turns each vector into vocabulary scores, left out of Kaplan's count), warmup length (how many early steps ramp the learning rate up from near zero) and scale-dependent optimizer tuning, which recovered Chinchilla's law. They also found careful learning-rate decay was *not* essential, contradicting explanation 1.

blocks.title: How the Kaplan exponent drifted to 0.73

scenes.caption: Kaplan et al. fitted the optimal-size exponent from their runs and got 0.73.
Pearce and Song: small scale plus non-embedding parameter counts bias the exponent upward.
Hoffmann et al. blamed the shared schedule; Porian et al. pointed to warmup, last-layer cost and optimizer tuning.
With those factors corrected, replications land near Chinchilla's 0.5 (Pearce and Song report 0.51).

blocks.md: Misconception: Kaplan's power laws were wrong. The loss-versus-size and loss-versus-data trends were real and still hold in shape. What shifted was the **compute-optimal allocation** derived from them, which is sensitive to experimental details. A scaling law is only as good as the runs it was fitted on.

blocks.question: GPT-3 used about 3.2e+23 FLOPs. Using $C \approx 6ND$ and Chinchilla's 20 tokens per parameter, what would a compute-optimal model at that budget look like?
options: 175B parameters on 300B tokens
About 500B parameters on 105B tokens
About 12B parameters on 4.3T tokens
About 51B parameters on 1.0T tokens
blocks.explain: Set $D = 20N$, so $C = 6 \cdot N \cdot 20N = 120N^2$ and $N = \sqrt{C/120} \approx 51$B, $D \approx 1.0$T. GPT-3's actual 175B on 300B tokens is the Kaplan-style choice; 12B on 4.3T overshoots the token ratio badly.

blocks.question: Which is the best summary of the Kaplan vs Chinchilla disagreement?
options: Chinchilla showed loss does not follow power laws
They agree that loss is a power law, but differ on how to split compute; replications trace Kaplan's split to experimental setup
Kaplan used more compute so its result is more reliable
The difference is only because they used different tokenizers
blocks.explain: Both papers find smooth power-law trends. The disagreement is the compute-optimal exponent (0.73 vs about 0.5), and later work explains it by schedule, parameter counting, small scale and optimizer details. Kaplan actually used smaller models than Chinchilla.

lessons.title: Batch size, learning rate and data limits as you scale

blocks.md: Lessons 3 to 5 chose the model size $N$ and the token count $D$. Every run has two more knobs, and a constraint the formulas so far ignore. A tiny example: a model will read 2T tokens. With a **batch** (tokens processed per optimizer step) of 4M tokens that is 500,000 steps; with 16M tokens it is 125,000 steps. If more accelerators process the bigger batch in about the same time per step, it finishes 4x sooner. But will 2T tokens still reach the same loss at the bigger batch? And what if you do not have 2T unique tokens at all?

McCandlish et al. (2018) answered the first question with the **gradient noise scale**. A minibatch gradient is the true gradient $G$ plus noise that shrinks as the batch grows. Their simple estimate is $B_{simple} = \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma)/|G|^2$: the summed variance of the per-example gradient components ($\Sigma$ is their covariance matrix, and the trace $\mathrm{tr}$ adds up its diagonal) divided by the squared length of the true gradient. With batches well below it, each step's gradient is mostly noise, and doubling the batch nearly halves the steps needed: perfect scaling. Well above it the gradient is already accurate, so a bigger batch barely cuts the steps and just burns tokens.

blocks.caption: McCandlish et al. Eqs. 2.11 and 2.12. To reach a fixed loss, steps S and examples processed E = BS trade off along a hyperbola. S_min is the fewest steps possible (huge batch); E_min the fewest examples (tiny batch).

blocks.md: Substitute $E = BS$ and solve: $S = S_{min}(1 + B_{crit}/B)$ and $E = E_{min}(1 + B/B_{crit})$. At $B = B_{crit}$, the **critical batch size**, you pay twice the minimum steps and twice the minimum data, which Kaplan et al. call a roughly optimal compromise between time and compute. McCandlish et al. predict $B_{crit}$ from the noise scale; the cheap $B_{simple}$ matched the measured critical batch at the order-of-magnitude level across most of their tasks, so you can estimate it from gradient statistics during training.

blocks.title: Steps vs data at a fixed target loss

scenes.caption: B = B_crit / 4: data-efficient (E = 1.25 E_min) but S = 5 S_min, the slowest in wall-clock.
B = B_crit: both are 2x their minimum. This is the knee of the curve.
B = 4 B_crit: steps fall only to 1.25 S_min, but data rises to 5 E_min, 2.5x the tokens of the critical batch for 37.5 percent fewer steps.
B = 8 B_crit: 9 E_min of data for 1.125 S_min of steps. Past the critical batch, extra batch is mostly wasted compute.

blocks.prompt: You train at exactly $B_{crit}$, then double the batch to $2B_{crit}$. How do the steps and the tokens needed to reach the same loss change?
blocks.reveal: Steps fall from $2S_{min}$ to $1.5S_{min}$, **25 percent fewer**. Tokens rise from $2E_{min}$ to $3E_{min}$, **50 percent more**. Far below the critical batch the same doubling would have nearly halved the steps for almost no extra tokens.

blocks.md:
Kaplan et al. measured the critical batch for their Transformers and found it depends on the loss reached, not directly on model size: $B_{crit}(L) \approx B_{*}/L^{1/\alpha_B}$ with $B_{*} \approx 2 \times 10^{8}$ tokens and $\alpha_B \approx 0.21$. It roughly doubles for every 13 percent drop in loss (simplified: the constants belong to their data and tokenizer). As a run trains, its loss falls, so the useful batch grows during the run.

That is why large runs grow the batch. GPT-3 raised it linearly from 32K tokens to the full size (3.2M tokens for the 175B model) over the first 4 to 12 billion tokens, and chose that size using the noise scale. Llama 3 405B used 4M tokens for the first 252M tokens for stability, then 8M, then 16M after 2.87T tokens for efficiency.

blocks.title: Kaplan's critical batch grows as loss falls

scenes.caption: B_crit = 2e8 / L^(1/0.21) tokens: 0.27M at a loss of 4, 1.07M at 3, 7.4M at 2. Loss values are on Kaplan's WebText2 scale.
From loss 4 to loss 2.5 the critical batch grows about 9x. A batch that suits the end of training wastes tokens at the start, which is one reason to ramp it up.

blocks.md: DeepSeek LLM (2024) fitted batch size and learning rate directly as power laws in compute. They grid-searched both at budgets from $10^{17}$ to $2 \times 10^{19}$ FLOPs, counted every setting within 0.25 percent of the best loss as near-optimal, and fitted $\eta_{opt} = 0.3118\,C^{-0.1250}$ and $B_{opt} = 0.2920\,C^{0.3271}$ ($B$ in tokens, $\eta$ the peak learning rate, $C$ in FLOPs counted their way: non-embedding FLOPs per token, attention included, times tokens). Bigger budgets get bigger batches and smaller learning rates, inside a broad near-optimal band. For their 7B model (about $8.5 \times 10^{22}$ FLOPs by their formula) the fit gives 9.2M tokens and $4.25 \times 10^{-4}$; they used 2,304 sequences of 4,096 tokens (9.4M) and $4.2 \times 10^{-4}$. They note this ties the batch to compute, unlike Kaplan and McCandlish, who tie it to the loss reached.

blocks.title: DeepSeek LLM's hyperparameter laws

scenes.caption: 1e17 FLOPs: batch 0.11M tokens, learning rate 2.3e-3.
1e19 FLOPs: 0.48M tokens, 1.3e-3.
About 8.5e22, DeepSeek 7B's budget: 9.2M tokens and 4.25e-4, next to the 9.4M and 4.2e-4 they used.
1e24, about their 67B budget: 20.7M tokens and 3.1e-4 (they used 18.9M and 3.2e-4). Over 7 decades the batch grows 195x while the learning rate falls 7.5x.

blocks.md: These laws carry hyperparameters across *compute*. To carry a tuned learning rate across *width*, use a parameterization built for it: the optional *muP* course covers one. Batch-size basics and gradient accumulation are in the *Training deep nets in practice* course.

**When unique data runs out.** Suppose you have 500B unique tokens, and lesson 3's rule says your budget wants a 100B model on 2T tokens ($C = 1.2 \times 10^{24}$ FLOPs). You could repeat the data 4 times, but is a repeated token worth a fresh one? Muennighoff et al. (2023) trained about 400 models, up to 9B parameters and 900B tokens, to find out. At a fixed compute budget, up to 4 **epochs** (passes over the data) changed the loss negligibly compared with unique data. With more repetition the value of extra compute decayed toward zero, and at 40 epochs repeating was worthless. They modelled this with an **effective data** size $D'$, the number of fresh tokens the repeated ones are worth:

blocks.tex: D' = U_D + U_D R_D^{*}\left(1 - e^{-R_D/R_D^{*}}\right), \qquad R_D = \text{epochs} - 1,\quad R_D^{*} \approx 15.4
blocks.caption: Muennighoff et al. Eq. 5. U_D: unique tokens. R_D: repetitions. R_D*, fitted, is roughly the half-life of repeated data. The same form for parameters beyond what the data can use gives R_N* about 5.3.

blocks.md: Read it as each repetition being worth a little less than the last. For small $R_D$ the bracket is about $R_D/R_D^{*}$, so $D' \approx U_D(1 + R_D) = D$: repeats count fully. For large $R_D$ it tends to 1, so $D'$ never exceeds $U_D(1 + R_D^{*})$, about 16.4 times the unique data, however long you train. At 4 epochs, $D' = 3.73\,U_D$: the 4 passes are worth 93 percent of 4 fresh ones.

blocks.title: Effective data when you repeat

scenes.caption: 4 epochs: 3.73 units of effective data for 4 processed. Almost as good as fresh.
16 epochs: 10.6 effective out of 16, about two thirds of the value.
40 epochs: 15.2. The cap is 16.4, so the next 60 epochs could add only about 1.2 more.

blocks.md: Back to 500B unique tokens and $1.2 \times 10^{24}$ FLOPs. Muennighoff et al.'s full fitted law (their Eq. 17, fitted on C4 web text, so only differences in loss matter) scores each split. Refusing to repeat, 500B tokens support only a 25B model at 20 tokens per parameter, which reaches 2.109. Spending the full budget is far better even with repeats: the planned 100B on 4 epochs reaches 2.024, just 0.007 nats worse than if all 2T tokens were fresh (2.017). The best constrained split is a bit smaller, about 84B on 2.39T tokens (4.8 epochs), at 2.0238, barely better. Going bigger hurts more: 200B on 2 epochs reaches 2.033. Excess parameters lose value faster than repeated data ($R_N^{*} \approx 5.3$ against $R_D^{*} \approx 15.4$), so when data is short, put extra compute into epochs before parameters.

blocks.title: Same budget, 500B unique tokens: extra loss per split

scenes.caption: If every token were fresh: loss above the best split (100B on 2T fresh tokens, 2.017), in thousandths of a nat, from Muennighoff et al.'s fitted law.
With only 500B unique tokens, every split loses a little and the valley shifts toward smaller models on more epochs. Larger models on fewer epochs lose most.

blocks.md: Two other ways to stretch data come from the same paper's tests on 19 downstream tasks. Filling up to half of the training data with Python code caused no drop on natural-language tasks. Perplexity filtering (keeping the 25 percent of documents a small model finds most predictable) and then repeating helped, while deduplication did not help in their benchmark. Their advice: use code and repetition, and reserve filtering for noisy datasets.

The critical batch size grows as loss falls: below it a bigger batch buys speed nearly free, above it you pay in tokens. When unique data is short, about 4 epochs cost almost nothing, value decays after that, and extra compute should go to epochs before parameters. All these constants come from one setup each: refit them with a small sweep (lesson 4).

blocks.question: Your run uses a batch 8 times the critical batch size. You cut it to exactly the critical batch. What happens to the tokens and steps needed to reach the same loss?
options: Both roughly halve
Tokens fall from about 9x to 2x the minimum, while steps rise from about 1.1x to 2x the minimum
Nothing changes; batch size only affects wall-clock time
Steps fall and tokens rise
blocks.explain: With $E = E_{min}(1 + B/B_{crit})$ and $S = S_{min}(1 + B_{crit}/B)$: at $8B_{crit}$, $E = 9E_{min}$ and $S = 1.125S_{min}$; at $B_{crit}$ both are 2x. You trade some wall-clock for 4.5x fewer tokens. Batch size changes the data needed, not just speed.

blocks.question: Early in a run the loss is 4.0; later it is 2.5. By Kaplan's fit, how did the critical batch size change, and what does that suggest?
options: It stayed fixed, because it depends only on model size
It fell, because a better model has smaller gradients and needs smaller batches
It doubled once, from 0.27M to 0.54M tokens
It grew about 9x (0.27M to 2.55M tokens), so a batch that suits late training wastes tokens early
blocks.explain: $B_{crit} \approx 2\times10^8/L^{1/0.21}$ tokens gives 0.27M at 4.0 and 2.55M at 2.5. It depends on the loss, not directly on size: as the true gradient shrinks relative to its noise, bigger batches stay useful. Hence the batch ramps in GPT-3 and Llama 3.

blocks.question: You have 300B unique tokens and compute for 3T tokens of training (10 epochs). Which plan does data-constrained scaling favour?
options: Repeat the data on a model somewhat smaller than the fresh-data optimum, accepting that later epochs are worth less
Train once on 300B tokens and leave 90 percent of the compute unused, since repeated data is worthless
Train a 10x larger model on one epoch, since extra parameters keep their full value
Use the fresh-data optimal model for 3T tokens, since repeats are exactly as good as fresh data
blocks.explain: At 10 epochs $D' \approx 7.8\,U_D$: repeats still add a lot, but less than fresh data would. Excess parameters decay faster than repeated data ($R_N^{*} \approx 5.3$ against $R_D^{*} \approx 15.4$), so the optimum shifts toward a smaller model on more epochs. Repeats are not worthless before roughly 40 epochs.

lessons.title: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break

blocks.md: Chinchilla minimizes **training** compute. But a deployed model is run for every token it serves, and a forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token. The LLaMA paper put it plainly: for a target level of performance, the preferred model is not the fastest to train but the fastest at inference. Its smallest model (6.7B parameters) was trained on 1T tokens, and the authors note a 7B model kept improving even after 1T tokens.

Sardana et al. (2024) made this precise. Fix the quality you need (a target loss $\ell$) and the number of tokens you expect to serve, $D_{inf}$. Then choose $N$ and training tokens $D_{tr}$ to minimize total lifetime compute:

blocks.caption: In words: pick the model size N and training tokens D_tr that minimize lifetime compute, 6 N D_tr to train plus 2 N D_inf to serve, while still reaching the target loss ell.

blocks.md: A worked example with the refit from lesson 3. Target the loss of the compute-optimal model at Gopher's budget: 1.974 (1.97444 before rounding). A smaller model can reach the same loss if it trains on more tokens. To find how many, fix $N$ and solve $L(N, D) = \ell$ for $D$: move everything except the data term to the other side, then undo the power $\beta$.

blocks.caption: In words: subtract the floor E and the model term from the target loss; what is left is the slack the data term must fit into. B divided by that slack, raised to 1 over beta, is the token count.

blocks.md:
One row by hand, $N$ = 50B. The model term is $482.01 / (5 \times 10^{10})^{0.3478} = 0.0916$. The slack is $1.97444 - 1.8172 - 0.0916 = 0.0656$, so $D = (2085.43 / 0.0656)^{1/0.3658} \approx 2.03$T tokens. The same steps give 72B: 1.33T, 40B: 2.81T, 30B: 4.82T.

Two warnings. If $E + A/N^{\alpha}$ is already above $\ell$, the slack is negative and there is **no solution**: the model is too small to reach that loss at any data size. Here that happens below about 10.6B parameters (a 10B model's floor is 1.9775). And because the slack is small, the answer is touchy: using the rounded target 1.974 moves the 50B row from 2.03T to 2.07T.

blocks.title: Lifetime compute for models of equal loss (units of 1e23 FLOPs)

scenes.caption: Training only. The compute-optimal 72B model is cheapest to train; 30B needs 1.51x the training compute for the same loss.
Add serving 10 trillion tokens at 2N FLOPs each. Now the 72B model is the most expensive in total, and 40B and 30B nearly tie for cheapest.
Serving 100 trillion tokens: inference dominates and the smallest model wins clearly, 68.68 vs 149.76.

blocks.prompt: Scanning all model sizes in this example, what is the cheapest choice when you expect to serve 10T tokens, and when you expect 100T?
blocks.reveal: At 10T served: about **34B parameters** on 3.7T tokens, about 109 tokens per parameter. At 100T served: about **21B** on 13.1T tokens, roughly 625 tokens per parameter. The more a model will be used, the further past 20 tokens per parameter it pays to train. This is called **overtraining** relative to Chinchilla.

blocks.md: Extreme ratios are extrapolations. Sardana et al. trained models up to 10,000 tokens per parameter and quality kept improving, but they also found that laws fitted at typical ratios **overestimate** the benefit of extra tokens at extreme ratios. Treat the hundreds-of-tokens-per-parameter numbers above as a direction, not a precise answer.

Real practice combines both ideas. For Llama 3, Meta ran scaling-law experiments from $6 \times 10^{18}$ to $10^{22}$ FLOPs with models from 40M to 16B parameters, fitted parabolas to each IsoFLOP curve and extrapolated to their 3.8e25 budget. The fit suggested 402B parameters on 16.55T tokens; they trained 405B on 15.6T. The smaller Llama 3 models were deliberately trained far longer than compute-optimal to be better at a fixed inference budget.

blocks.title: Llama 3: from small runs to a flagship forecast

nodes.label:
Power law: optimal
tokens vs compute

scenes.caption: Cheap runs at many sizes and budgets supply the data. Each IsoFLOP curve gets a parabola; its minimum is the compute-optimal model for that budget.
A power law through those minima, extrapolated about 3.5 orders of magnitude, sets the flagship's size and token count.

Loss is not accuracy, so a second chain maps compute to benchmark negative log-likelihood (the loss on the correct answer), then NLL to accuracy with a sigmoid. Meta reports it slightly underestimated the flagship's final score.

blocks.md: OpenAI reported something similar for GPT-4: a fit of the form $L(C) = aC^b + c$ (fresh fitted constants, not lesson 3's exponents; $c$ is an irreducible floor like $E$) to runs using at most 10,000x less compute predicted GPT-4's final loss with high accuracy. Scaling laws are now used as an engineering forecast before committing a large budget.

Scaling laws are no longer fitted only to pretraining loss:

- **Downstream metrics.** Llama 3's two-step chain above maps compute to benchmark NLL, then NLL to accuracy.
- **Architectures.** Clark et al. (2022) fitted unified scaling laws for routed (mixture-of-experts) models, where parameter count and compute per token become two separate axes. The optional *Fine-grained MoE* course covers these models.
- **Inference-time compute.** Snell et al. (2024) scaled the compute spent per prompt. A compute-optimal test-time strategy was more than 4x more efficient than best-of-N sampling, and in a FLOPs-matched comparison it let a small model beat a 14x larger one on problems the small model could already sometimes solve. The optional *Test-time compute scaling* course covers this.

Where they break or mislead:

- **Loss is not ability.** Schaeffer et al. (2023) argue many reported **emergent abilities**, sudden jumps at some scale, come from nonlinear metrics like exact-match accuracy. With continuous metrics the same models improve smoothly.
- **Data runs out.** Muennighoff et al. (2023) found up to 4 epochs of repeated data is nearly as good as fresh data; beyond that the value of more compute decays toward zero. Lesson 6 works through what to do about it.
- **Fits are fragile.** The rounded constants in the Chinchilla paper give an optimum at Gopher's budget of 32B parameters on 3.0T tokens by our calculation (93 tokens per parameter), inconsistent with the paper's other methods. Besiroglu et al. traced this to an optimizer that stopped early and rounding, the failure lesson 4 reproduced.

blocks.title: Optimal tokens per parameter: two fits of one formula

scenes.caption: The 20-to-1 rule from Chinchilla's Approaches 1 and 2, and the 70B on 1.4T model they trained.
Plugging the published, rounded Approach 3 constants into the closed form: the ratio climbs from about 32 to 153 across this range, contradicting the 20 they used.
The refit of the same formula stays near 20 (24 down to 16). Same functional form, different fitted constants, very different advice.

blocks.md: Chinchilla-optimal answers one question: lowest loss per training FLOP. Real decisions also weigh inference volume, available data and downstream metrics, so production models are often smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter.

blocks.question: A teammate wants a 10B model to hit the 1.974 target by training longer. With the refit, $E + A/N^{\alpha}$ is 1.9775 for 10B. What does the inversion formula give?
options: A very large but finite D, around 100T tokens
About 20 tokens per parameter, so 200B tokens
No solution: the slack is negative, so no amount of data reaches 1.974
D = 0, because the model already beats the target
blocks.explain: The slack $1.974 - 1.9775$ is negative, so $B$ divided by it has no real power that gives a token count. Even infinite data only removes the data term; the loss stays at or above 1.9775. The 20-to-1 rule is about compute-optimal training, not about reaching a fixed loss.

blocks.question: A team will serve its model to millions of users for a year and needs a fixed quality bar. What does inference-aware scaling recommend?
options: Train the Chinchilla-optimal model, since it reaches the bar with the least compute
Train a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal, paying extra training compute to cut serving cost
Train the largest model the budget allows on fewer tokens, since bigger models are more sample-efficient
Train any size; inference cost does not depend on model size
blocks.explain: Serving costs about 2N FLOPs per token, so with heavy usage a smaller model that reaches the same loss by training longer has lower lifetime cost. Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute only. Bigger-and-shorter is Kaplan's advice and makes serving more expensive.

blocks.question: Exact-match accuracy on a task jumps from near 0% to 60% between two model sizes, while per-token loss falls smoothly. What is the most careful reading?
options: The larger model suddenly acquired a new capability that scaling laws cannot describe
The metric is nonlinear: smooth per-token gains compound into an all-or-nothing score, so the jump may be partly a metric effect
The loss measurement must be wrong
The smaller model was undertrained, which fully explains the jump
blocks.explain: Schaeffer et al. show that discontinuous metrics like exact match can turn smooth improvement into apparent jumps, and continuous metrics make the trend smooth again. That is why Llama 3 forecast accuracy through NLL first. It does not prove no real change ever happens, but the jump alone is not evidence of one.
